title: You Are Altogether Beautiful: The Bride and Her Garden
summary: The man praises his bride's beauty from her eyes to her breasts in a series of vivid images, declaring that she is altogether beautiful and without flaw. He calls her to come with him from the mountains of Lebanon and tells her that she has captured his heart. He then pictures her as a garden locked up and a fountain sealed, full of fruits and spices, and she answers by inviting him to come into his garden.
story: Chapter 3 ended with Solomon's wedding procession and the king crowned on the day of his heart's rejoicing. Chapter 4 continues the wedding theme: for the first time the man calls the woman my bride (verse 8), a title that appears six times in 4:8-5:1 and nowhere else in the Song. This is the heart of the Song's central section and, for many readers, the wedding night pictured in poetry. The chapter's movement is from praise to invitation, from the man's admiration of his bride to her welcome of him into the garden, a scene that reaches its fulfillment in the first verse of chapter 5.
historical: The chapter's places span the land of Israel and beyond. Gilead (verse 1) was the hilly, pastoral region east of the Jordan, known for its flocks. Lebanon, Amana, Senir, and Hermon (verse 8) are the mountains of the far north; Deuteronomy 3:9 notes that the Amorites called Hermon Senir, and Amana appears to be a peak in the Anti-Lebanon range. These mountains were remote, rugged, and home to wild animals, which is why the man pictures his bride as coming down from the dens of lions and leopards. The tower of David (verse 4) is not known from any other text or excavation, and it may be a real fortification in Jerusalem or a poetic image of strength and dignity. Warriors' shields were sometimes hung on city walls and towers as a display of strength, as Ezekiel 27:11 describes at Tyre.
cultural:
Verses 1 to 7 are an example of a descriptive love poem that praises the beloved's body part by part, often called by the Arabic term wasf by scholars who have compared it with later Arabic wedding songs. The Song contains four such poems (4:1-7; 5:10-16; 6:4-7; 7:1-9). To a modern reader some of the images sound odd, but each makes a specific point of comparison. Hair like goats streaming down Gilead pictures dark, flowing movement, since the goats of the region were black. Teeth like newly shorn sheep, each with its twin, praise white, complete, even teeth, in a world where many adults had lost some. Her neck like the tower of David praises her upright bearing and perhaps her jewelry. The images are meant to be felt, not pictured literally.

The man calls her my sister, my bride (verses 9 to 12). Sister was a common term of affection for a beloved in ancient Near Eastern love poetry, including Egyptian love songs, where lovers call each other sister and brother; it has nothing to do with family relation. The locked garden and sealed fountain (verse 12) picture exclusivity and chastity: a private garden in the ancient world was walled and locked, and a sealed spring was reserved for its owner. Proverbs 5:15-18 uses similar images of a well and a fountain for faithful married love. The spices of verses 13 and 14 include nard and cinnamon, imported from far to the east, and saffron, calamus, myrrh, and aloes; together they describe a garden of unimaginable luxury.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 7 are the man's descriptive praise, framed by the words how beautiful you are (verse 1) and you are altogether beautiful (verse 7), a technique called inclusio. The description moves downward from eyes to hair, teeth, lips, brow, neck, and breasts, and it stops with reserve, turning to the image of the mountain of myrrh (verse 6). Verses 8 to 11 are an invitation and a declaration of love, built on repetition (my sister, my bride; come with me from Lebanon). Verses 12 to 15 develop the garden image, and verse 16 is the woman's answer, in which she invites the winds to blow on her garden and her beloved to come into it. The movement from his garden to my garden to his garden again, in verse 16 and 5:1, shows her gift of herself to him.

outline.t: How beautiful you are: the man praises his bride
You have captured my heart, my sister, my bride
A garden locked up, a fountain sealed
The bride's invitation: let my beloved come into his garden

doctrines.note: The chapter pictures the joy of a husband and wife in each other on their wedding day. The locked garden opened only to her husband expresses the exclusivity of married love, and her invitation shows that the gift is freely given, not taken.

The garden imagery echoes Eden, where God placed the man and woman and they were naked and unashamed (Genesis 2:25). The Song pictures married love as a return to that original goodness, full of fruit, fragrance, and delight.

The sealed fountain speaks of purity and faithfulness. The Song treats sexual love not as something shameful but as something set apart for one person, which is close to what the Bible means by holy: reserved and devoted.

words.note: Kallah, bride. It appears five times in chapter 4 and once more in 5:1, and nowhere else in the Song. The word can mean daughter-in-law in other contexts, since a bride joined her husband's family. Its concentration in these verses is one reason many readers take 4:1-5:1 as the wedding and wedding night at the center of the Song.

Achot, sister. In verses 9, 10, and 12 the man calls the woman my sister, my bride. In ancient Near Eastern love poetry sister was a term of affection and equality, suggesting closeness and familiarity. It expresses that she is both his beloved and his closest companion.

Gan, garden. It appears four times in this chapter. The garden was a place of beauty, fruitfulness, and delight, and in Genesis it is the place where God placed the first man and woman. The Song's garden is a picture of the woman herself, lush, fragrant, and fruitful, reserved for her beloved and opened to him by her own invitation.

Naal, to lock or bar. In verse 12 the garden is locked up, a picture of the bride's chastity and exclusive devotion to her husband. The image is not of a prison but of something precious kept for the right person. The locking gives the opening in verse 16 its meaning.

christ: The New Testament does not quote this chapter. The connections Christians have drawn come through the Bible's theme of the church as Christ's bride. Paul writes that Christ gave himself up for the church to present her to himself in splendor, holy and without blemish (Ephesians 5:25-27), which many readers have heard as an echo of the man's words that his bride is altogether beautiful and without flaw (4:7). The echo is thematic, not a quotation. The garden also connects with the Bible's larger story, which begins in a garden (Genesis 2), turns at a garden where Jesus prayed and was arrested (John 18:1), finds its resurrection morning in a garden near the tomb (John 19:41; 20:15), and ends in a restored paradise with the river of life and the tree of life (Revelation 22:1-2). Christian tradition has read the locked garden as the church or the believer's soul, kept for Christ alone. Whether one reads the chapter allegorically or as human love poetry, the pattern is the same: love that is faithful, delighted, and self-giving.

hard.q: How should a modern reader handle the chapter's frank praise of the body?
hard.a: The chapter praises a woman's beauty in physical detail, and some readers find that embarrassing in a book of Scripture. Several points help. First, the language is poetic and restrained: it uses images rather than explicit description, and it treats the body with admiration rather than crudeness. Second, the setting is a wedding, where the man calls the woman my bride, so the praise belongs within the covenant of marriage. Third, the Bible does not treat the body as shameful; God made it and called it good, and Genesis 2 ends with the man and woman naked and unashamed. Allegorical readers, ancient and modern, have often read the imagery as describing the beauty of God's people, and some have been uncomfortable with a literal reading. Many readers today think the literal and the spiritual readings can coexist: the chapter honors married love and the body as God's good gifts, and in doing so it points beyond itself. The Song models a way of speaking about sexuality that is neither coy nor coarse, but grateful.

questions: The man praises his bride as altogether beautiful. How might words of honest admiration strengthen a marriage or a friendship?
The locked garden pictures love reserved for one person. What does faithfulness look like in your relationships, and what helps protect it?
How does it affect your view of the body to see it praised so openly in Scripture?
